utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Russo, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Corn, perhaps needless to remind you, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, but that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by clarifying a few answers from yesterday. At transcript page 21.223, line 13, I asked you to confirm that you had not considered the documents listed in paragraph 12 of D1644, your supplemental information sheet, prior to drafting your addendum. And you answered that, as a general proposition, that was correct. Then I asked whether you were provided with any information beyond those documents and beyond the evidence of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings and Marko Rajic, and you answered: "Well, I can't immediately correlate the number with the document. Can I tell you other information that I have considered in my preparation to come over here. There was a transcript from a meeting between the president and members of the military staff, including the General. I think it was in Brioni. I looked at that. There were some psychological operations directive that looked at, related to information to influence the conduct of the civilian population. Rajcic's testimony was something that I looked at extensively. As I said, the visual disposition of military objectives in Knin was obviously something that was important in my mind. So, I mean, that's a candid offer of the -- of the information that I think had a significant influence on my thought process." So your answer began with an identification of documents you considered in your preparation to come over here, which suggests to me, at least, that it was just testimony preparation. But your answer ended with a comment about the information which had a significant influence on your thought process, which led me to believe that you had considered it before reaching your conclusions. So it's still unclear to me whether you considered the Brioni transcript, the testimony of Marko Rajic, and the psychological operations directives before you drafted the addendum. Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were not -- that was not information that I relied on when I drafted my addendum. Just to clarify, I'm trying to be as -- as forthcoming as I possibly can. I could not have drafted the addendum without having some context about the overall concept of the operation. I think I made that point yesterday. To be -- from my perspective, I don't know how any expert on the use of a method or means of warfare in the context of an operation could render an opinion without knowing the general nature of the operation. For example, when I look at Colonel Konings's addendum, it's based on a list of assumptions, hypothetical assumptions. It's a response to hypothetical assumptions. But it seems relatively clear to me that he is applying those assumptions within the broader context of the operation, because those assumptions don't include every aspect of Operation Storm. And so what I was trying to convey was that I wrote the addendum based on the facts and assumptions provided by counsel with the addition of that one fact that I was made aware of in the meeting in Tampa that I wanted to -- I thought was so significant that I wanted to make sure it was before the Tribunal. And that was the effort I made with Defence counsel was to allow me to see from their perspective the facts and assumptions related to the operation that they believed were before the Tribunal. But I also don't think that I could have expunged from my -- from my thought process the general concept of the operation itself, and that's the point I was trying to make. The information that was referred to in the last paragraph that you recited from the record was information that I used as I prepared to come over as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm not faulting you for relying on some context that you received during the oral presentation, but, of course, you understand that this leaves the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution at a bit of an informational disadvantage in terms of what you actually had in your mind when you drafted the addendum. So getting back to that oral presentation, who exactly made the presentation to you?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It were -- in that meeting there were the three attorneys representing the defendant, who are in the courtroom today, and there was an individual named Goran who is -- who was one of their technical advisors on the operational aspects of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present beside yourself?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and those four individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And during that presentation, Professor, were you told about or shown any evidence concerning incidents of shelling by General Gotovina's forces in civilian-populated areas of the RSK prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you told about or shown any evidence concerning incidents of burning or looting of Serb property by General Gotovina's forces prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you told about or shown any evidence concerning President Tudjman's or any other Croatian government official's views on the desirability of Serbs remaining in or returning to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that -- I believe there was a discussion of a meeting that occurred with the president and members of the military staff, including the General. Whether or not that was discussed in Tampa I can't say without absolute certainty. Obviously I already told you that I have seen the transcript of that meeting, and I don't know even if that transcript would fall within the category of the question you ask, reflecting his views on the desirability of members of the Serb population to leave or return. I know there's some discussion of Serbs leaving the operational area around Knin, but, to my recollection, I don't think -- I understood that as a statement on his view on the desirability of their return or not, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I just want to see if I understand you correctly. You're referring to the Brioni meeting.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you're indicating that you don't recall whether that came up during the December 2008 oral presentation but you certainly recall that from your review of that transcript after you drafted the addendum.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it may have come up in that meeting. I just -- honestly I can't recall whether or not that's where I first learned of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Other than that particular meeting at Brioni, were you given any information about any other meetings between President Tudjman, other government officials, in which a desirability of Serbs remaining in or returning to Croatia was discussed?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only other -- the only other source of information that relates to that were some psychological operations directives that I reviewed prior to coming to The Hague to testify, but that was well after the addendum had been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell us what those psychological operations directives, what you recall from them?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I recall most significantly was I was reviewing one which was, I think, an opinion of somebody reviewing those reports rendering this -- this person - I think it was a transcript of testimony - this person was giving an opinion as to the General's reaction or, I guess, endorsement of some psychological operation concepts or directives. What I recall about it was a note that I put on the side of that indicated I didn't believe that the conclusion that was reached in this opinion was accurate, based on the comment that was embedded in the transcript from General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Was this a transcript of the testimony of a witness who testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you have any idea which witness that was?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you shown the transcripts of testimony of any other witness besides Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, Marko Rajic, and this individual whom you've just mentioned that you can't recall?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: During the oral presentation given to you in late December 2008 were you told about or shown any evidence concerning the takeover of UN observation posts by General Gotovina's forces during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, were you provided with or have you reviewed any of the filings in this case?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed -- other than the report that Colonel Konings made, which I assume was filed as an expert report, and my own, which was filed as a report, those are the only filings, I believe, I have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you told anything about the Prosecution's allegations or positions in this case?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told in preparation for testimony, after -- well, after the addendum was filed, probably within the last month, I was provided a very general overview of what the Defence counsel believe was the Prosecution's theory. Or let be me more precise. The relationship between -- let me -- let me -- obviously my focus has been on the use of artillery during Operation Storm, particularly in the town of Knin, and the discussion was to place this aspect of the case into broader context and how the Defence felt it was connected to the broader series of charges against the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you could, please, tell us what the Defence told you in that respect.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that I had emphasised to them as -- in preparation to come over and testify -- well, not emphasise. I wanted to ensure that the focus of my testimony was limited to the subject matter of the reports, which was the use of artillery and the legality of use of artillery under the assumptions and facts that had been provided. They validated that. They said that the defendant was facing charges for a pattern of misconduct alleged to have been committed by forces under his command, and that the use of artillery, they believed, if it was determined to be illegal, would be an element in essentially connecting the broader pattern of misconduct to the defendant's intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you told anything else specifically about what the Prosecution's position is about why the artillery attack was illegal?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously from Colonel Konings's report there's a fairly -- a fairly clear manifestation that the Prosecution believes that the -- the factual basis for the allegations of improper use of artillery were effects and aspects of the targets that were -- that diverged from many of the facts and assumptions that were the foundation of my report. So, in that regard, just reading the facts and assumptions in the letter that you signed reveals to me, or revealed to me, a fairly obvious basis for why the Prosecution would allege that the use of artillery -- artillery was improper. And in several discussions with Defence counsel, they -- they told me of evidence that they believed or -- generally, facts they believed were more consistent with the Prosecution's theory than the facts and assumptions that I had relied on. And essentially those -- those facts were in line with the facts and assumptions that you provided to Colonel Konings in the hypotheticals that you asked him to base his opinion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused by the last part of your answer, but I understand that you may have received an impression of what the Prosecution's theory was based on Colonel Konings's report. But my question to you was what you were told by the Defence about what the Prosecution's theory of unlawful attack was.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me give you an example. The -- as I've told you several times, when I wrote that addendum, I was obviously -- I obviously felt it was important that the facts and assumptions that I was basing those opinions on were relatively well established in the record, and I asked the Defence to validate that on several occasions. And on several occasions in those discussions, the Defence would say, Now, obviously the Prosecution is not going to agree or probably will not agree with all the facts and assumptions that we're providing. For example, their view is that there was a much more widespread use of indirect fire in a random kind of chaotic pattern throughout the city of Knin. So in that regard, I -- I really didn't need them to tell me that, because that was embedded within the hypotheticals of Colonel Konings's addendum, and those hypotheticals were provided by the Prosecution, so I assumed those were facts and assumptions that the Prosecution feels have been well established by the record. But if that is a statement by the Defence on evidence related to the Prosecution's theory, then those were discussions we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were you told anything else by the Defence specifically regarding the allegations of unlawful attack not connected to what you read in Colonel Konings's report?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the only other information, I think, that would fall into that category would be the Defence assessment of conclusions that they believe the Prosecution would draw from certain evidence. For example, in the -- in some of the information provided to Colonel Konings there -- or even in one of the hypotheticals in the letter that you sent to him, there's reference to a hospital being on a target list, and the Defence would say that the Prosecution likely believes or, We expect that the Prosecution believes that that is an indication of improper intent, because a hospital shouldn't be on a target list. But, again, that is in the hypothetical that you proffered to Colonel Konings. So it was -- the discussions of Prosecution theory were always nested or connected, if you will, to my assessments, the assessments I was providing them of my opinion on propriety of listing targets in a targeting annex, of engaging certain targets within the city, and most of that is in the addendum that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you have given us an example or two. I'm looking for as comprehensive an account as can you give us, regarding what you were told about the Prosecution's, either allegations, positions or questions likely to be put to you. Can you tell me everything you recall about being told about those things by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will start with the last one. In terms of questions to be put to me, the Defence said, Obviously you should expect the Prosecution to challenge both some of the facts and assumptions upon which the addendum was -- the opinions in the addendum were based and perhaps the strength of the -- or the credibility of the opinions themselves, even if the facts and assumptions are accurate. There was -- as I said, there was discussion of differing views on the -- on the objective evidence of where artillery strikes were -- were being made, that the Defence expected the Prosecution to assert or to suggest, whatever term you want to use, that there was a much more widespread or chaotic pattern of indirect fire within Knin. There was discussion of whether or not I believed a corps-level command post would cease to be an important objective, if the commander was not present, based on, I think, a question that might have been proffered to another witness during the trial by the Prosecution, and as I recall that's a question that Defence counsel asked me yesterday in direct testimony. There was discussion of, I believe, testimony from witnesses, perhaps UN operatives, that were in Knin that referred to artillery strikes occurring everywhere within the city of Knin, and that was brought to my attention to ask my opinion of -- is -- do I think there's an explanation for that. I already mentioned the church --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I want to stop you right there before you move on. I'd like to know exactly what you were told about these UN operatives and whatever opinion you were asked about and what opinion you, in fact, provided.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was told that -- as I recall, I was told that there had been a witness or maybe a report - I don't know - from an individual or individuals working for the UN in Knin who said that, from their observation perspective, there were artillery rounds exploding all over the city, creating the inference that the use of artillery was as chaotic as is suggested in the hypotheticals that you provided to Colonel Konings in the report. And they didn't really get much further than that because I interrupted them at that point, and I said, Well, I'm not surprised that that is the perception because looking at the aerial photographs that I saw from the beginning of the meeting in Tampa, there were military objectives dispersed all over the city by the enemy forces. So if I'm watching this attack from a distance or from a vantage point, it will look like there are rounds exploding all over the city because there were objectives all over the city. And I -- I mean, I cut them off at that point because that was my reaction to that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to explore that a little bit. First of all, I understand that your interpretation that if somebody's is looking at the town and they're saying that the town is being shelled all over and from your perspective there are military targets all over, one interpretation of that, which is apparently your interpretation, is that they are mistaking shelling all over the town with shelling of military targets all over the town. That's -- that's your perspective of that testimony. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't. I wasn't there. I didn't observe what happened. What I said to the Defence was, There are multiple inferences you could draw from that evidence. One inference would be there was a chaotic, random, indiscriminate attack of an entire city. But an alternate inference, which I believe would be reasonable, based on the dispersion of military objectives by the Serb forces within Knin, is that there's an effort to target military objectives that are scattered throughout the city and it's creating the visual impression of a random indiscriminate attack. So I actually told them -- in fact I specifically recall using the language of multiple reasonable inferences to draw from that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I want to be clear about that. You're not suggesting in any way that one interpretation is any more reasonable than the other, and you're not leaning towards them being mistaken about random shelling or them being correct about random shelling. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- as I say, I was not present. I do know this. It's not clear to me that the individuals rendering that opinion were aware of the dispersion of military objectives within the city. When I heard the Defence tell me about that opinion, I was aware of that and so that triggered my reaction. I don't -- I just think there are multiple inferences you can draw from that perception. I don't know which one is right and which one is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You say it's not clear to you that the individuals rendering that opinion were aware of the dispersion of military objectives within the city. Did you have any reason to think that they weren't?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- all I know is I was told that there were individuals who worked for the UN who said it looked like the entire city was being attacked by artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did they tell that you some of these individuals had, in fact, travelled through the town of Knin during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that -- as a matter of fact, there was one they -- that I recall them saying was driving around the city, I think, evacuating people or trying to assist in evacuation while the shelling was occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And were you given any information about whether the individuals making these observations were able to tell the difference between fire for effect, corrected fire, and simply random fire?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I was told was that there were UN personnel who observed the attack and said that it looked like the entire city was being attacked. Now, if -- there was no discussion of whether they were making -- that their -- their testimony or their report made reference to technical aspects of the artillery fire. And those three terms you provide, fire for effect, for example, okay, you can't make an opinion about fire for effect without knowing the effect that the fire is intended to achieve. So what effect was intended by that fire? My expectation or assumption would be, if I'm observing the effects of an attack, the kinetic effect of an artillery attack, I don't have full situational knowledge of what operational effect the commander intends to achieve with that artillery. I just see the kinetic effect. So when you say, Did they tell you whether or not these individuals perceived whether it was for effect, adjustment or random, no. There was no discussion of that. But I would assume they wouldn't be able to assess whether it was for effect because they were unlikely privy to the operational planning that defined the effect the commander wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your answer makes me think you're misunderstanding what I mean by fire for effect. That's a term that was used by several of the witnesses here to indicate a delivery of multiple projectiles at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to that assessment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there was an objection against the way in which you summarise what witnesses said, you have to be more specific, Mr. Russo, if you want to pursue this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, then let me just put it to you, when I said "fire for effect," that's what I'm talking about. The difference between the single shot attempting to get closer to a target and then the multiple number of rounds which are fired once it appears that the target or believes they have come close enough in targeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Then it's irrelevant because Mr. Russo's position on that score is of no consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is part of his question. So if he asked the witness and -- unless you say that the whole question using this term is irrelevant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do. Except it's relevant for the Chamber, I submit, as it ties back to what a particular witnesses says and not what Mr. Russo opines. That's the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The term used in the question by Mr. Russo could confuse. Therefore, Mr. Russo is entitled to explain what he meant by that. Whether that is what witnesses said or not is a different matter for the Chamber to review. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, do you understand what I mean now when I say fire for effect?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I understand. And, again, I would emphasise that I think it's -- it -- it is -- it is not a reflection of the operational characteristics of employment of artillery. What you're talking about is a classic kind of vernacular that relates to identifying a target where you believe, as the commander, that you can achieve an effect you desire by putting a large volume of artillery rounds on the target. So the observer identifies the target, calls fire, the initial round or several rounds, the initial salvo strikes, and from that strike, the observer adjusts fire and then calls a -- a phrase we use called "fire for effect." But, you see, that presumes that the effect that the commander seeks to achieve with that fire mission is a destructive effect, and it is very possible that the commander might not seek to achieve a destructive effect. And in fact from my review, and if you look at the assumptions and facts in my addendum, it is relatively clear that General Gotovina and his artillery staff were aware that they were under serious ammunition resupply constraint, and that he had made the judgement that the priority of effort would be the tactical point of attack in order to support the breach of the Serb defensive positions. Therefore, the use of artillery against military objectives in Knin was conducted based on an economy of force principle, and so the effect that he sought to achieve there in most cases probably was not destruction. So your question presupposes that these did -- would these witnesses have been able to notice whether it was a fire for effect, but you're assuming that the effect that the witnesses assumed the General wanted to achieve was destruction, and I don't believe that they would have known whether or not that was the effect. So two or three rounds may indeed have been intended to achieve the effect of the fire in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I think I understand what you're saying, Professor. But that answer, at least from my perspective and correct me if I'm wrong, assumes that these UN observers did not in fact see fire for effect, that they did not in fact see clumped together projectiles landing on a particular target after a corrected fire. Let me just finish here. It sounds like what you're saying is that General Gotovina was not intending to destroy targets, so therefore, he wouldn't be firing a high volume of projectiles on any particular target. And therefore anybody observing that would not see what I'm calling fire for effect and would assume that it's simply random shelling with the single odd shell here or there. Do I have that last part right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the question that I responded to was your question, Do I understand what you mean by fire for effect, right? And that was my response of my understanding of what I thought you meant by fire for effect. I will reiterate the underlying point in response to the last part of your question. I don't believe that the people observing the kinetic effect of artillery fires in Knin would have had full knowledge of the operational effect that was intended by those strikes. Now, it's clear to me and it's obvious from the addendum, for example, that the headquarters was a high-priority target, because of its command, control, communication, and intelligence function. So it would be unsurprising for me to find out that people that observed the attack on Knin saw something that fit more within your definition of fire for effect in and around the headquarters than perhaps in other areas. But my point is that if -- yes, to answer your question, I think it would be a rational assumption by somebody observing the kinetic effect that a salve of rounds into a certain area that was not followed by a substantially heavier attack or salvo would seem inconsistent with their assumption that the first salvo was for correction purposes. But my point is, they don't know whether the first salvo was for correction purposes or was for effect itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's clear now. Thank you. Now, you're told that an opinion by people who actually witnessed the attack was that they believed it was random shots all over the town, and if I understand you correctly, you stopped the Defence at that point and interjected your own sense of why that might be correct or why it might be incorrect, or what inferences could be drawn from that or not drawn from that. What I'm more interested in is whether you asked for any evidence about that. It seems to me that if somebody tells you, Well, a precipient witness to the event said it looked to them like it was random and all over the town that you would want information. Well, I'd like to though, first of all, if that person knew what the targets were; I'd like to know how many people said that; I'd like it know, as you say, whether they had any knowledge of the operational objectives; I'd like to know what their particular expertise is in making these things. Did you ask any of these questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the form. I mean, if it was a question, I object to the format of giving a speech to the witness and then delivering a question that doesn't necessarily tie it together, so it's a -- my objection is to form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Russo would like to know, Mr. Corn, is the following. You apparently stopped the Defence giving an explanation of what would be a rational explanation and which may have indicated that those observing were perhaps misinterpreting what happened. Now, Mr. Russo's question apparently is why did you stop them, why didn't you ask for further information on that moment, what did they know, et cetera? That's apparently what Mr. Russo wants to find out. Mr. Russo, if I'm understanding your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information I was given was not information that matches the characterisation of the summary provided by Mr. Russo in his question. I was told that there were people who worked for the UN who said that it looked like the entire city was under attack. Not that there were random attacks, not that there was random use of artillery. They said it looked like the entire city was under attack. That's what I was told. And I, at that point, maybe it's just -- you know, maybe it was -- I got a little bit excited, I don't know. I said -- it was like something popped in my head. Because I had already known that there were military objectives all through the city and I said, Well, there's a logical explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think what Mr. Russo is asking you is that -- a one-liner, it looked like, as if. I think in view of your experience, you would have known that that would not have been the whole of the testimony of that witness, that he would have told us that he been asked not only about what it looked like, but what he observed and perhaps also what he knew, where he was exactly, whether he travelled around. I mean, all kind of detailed questions, which -- of which the answers would have served someone to test the possible explanation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you had on your mind. And Mr. Russo would like to know why you stopped immediately on the basis of the one-liner, and why you didn't further explore on what basis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- such a -- it looked as if was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. When I say I interrupted them, I interrupted them when they made the comment about it looked like the entire city was under attack. I think subsequently to that I did ask, Where were they? And that's when I learned there was one individual that was driving around the city, I think I was told he was trying to collect refugees or assist in the evacuation of refugees, and then others were in a building watching the attack that was on the periphery of the -- it wasn't in the city centre, as I recall. And that -- and I do remember thinking, well, the vision they have would create that perception. But in retrospect I would -- I think the reason that that was the -- all the information that I felt I wanted was because they were there, I wasn't, and I'm not contradicting necessarily the inference they drew from what they observed. All I was doing was pointing out to the Defence that I believed that, based on the dispersion of military objectives within the city, there would be a possible alternate explanation for that conclusion. And that's where we left it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in response to His Honour Judge Orie's question, draft transcript page 19, lines 18 to 19, you said: "I was told that there were people who worked for the UN who said that it looked like the entire city was under attack, not that were random attacks, not that there was some random use of artillery." Now, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that if the entire city was under attack, that's an indiscriminate attack. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on what military objectives were in the city and where they were. My point was, they didn't tell me that these witnesses said there were random attacks or indiscriminate attacks. They said these witnesses or the report - I honestly can't remember whether it was a witness or a report - said their perception was the entire city was under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I -- the point I'm trying to make here is what you were told about what they perceived would have put you on some notice that this sounds like something that should be investigated.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if my understanding of the enemy disposition up to that point was that there was one military objective in the city, let's say the corps headquarters, and then there's a witness that says, It looked like the entire city was under attack, then that obviously would raise a very significant concern. But I -- I think that my reaction to that was based on my belief, based on what I had been shown and what I looked at and the assumptions and facts related to my opinion, that the enemy had located within Knin military objectives throughout the city. They were not isolated to one kazerne [phoen] or one specific area of the city. There were military objectives throughout the city, and the enemy, because of his locating some high-value targets within the city, would have created the impression in the mind of his opponent that the city was -- he was treating the city as something that was worth protecting. And so I -- what I did is I imagined the perception of what it would look like to see the kinetic effect of high-explosive artillery rounds that are being directed at enemy military objectives dispersed in a -- throughout a city, and that's what made me say there's probably or I think there is an alternate explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, based on what you know about the dispersion of the military objectives throughout the town, is it your testimony that it would have been lawful to shell the entire town in order to strike those military objectives? Because it sounds like to me that that's what you're suggesting. I would like your answer on that.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I'd refer you back to my initial report. The answer to that is a categorical no. It is clearly prohibited by international humanitarian law to treat a series of dispersed military objectives within a populated area as one large objective. That was the product of Additional Protocol I's rejection of a practice of carpet bombing during the Second World War, and in the view of many, carpet bombing by the United States during the war against North Vietnam. And it is -- it's a -- as a fundamental tenet of international humanitarian law that is illicit and improper to simply place an entire populated area in the cross-hairs because the enemy has dispersed military objectives within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And based on what you know about the dispersion of targets in Knin you'll agree with me, won't you, that there are parts of the town which are not within the probable range of error around the military objectives within the town. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are certainly parts of the town that do not qualify as lawful military objectives. Now your reference to probable range of error I think raises another issue. You raise that issue in -- as I recall, in the letter that requests the addendum by Colonel Konings --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me -- I'm sorry, Professor. I'll give you an opportunity to give me your answer or your views about that, but first I just want an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer your question without endorsing what I think is your view of probable error --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, I'll --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I'm not sure I agree with that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm going give you an opportunity to explain your disagreement with that. But what I'm asking you is what you know about the military objectives, the location of the alleged military objectives in the town, if you drew around those, the probable range of error of the weaponry being fired at them, would it encompass the entirety of the town?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if -- if I may, that certainly wasn't the first question, but if we're getting into probable range of error, that is an interesting concept that the Prosecution itself offered no evidence on during its case, zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is that an objection or a comment, Mr. President? I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's an objection concerning the Prosecution's case concerning probable range of error which they had a burden to present to this Trial Chamber if they thought it was an issue. It is simply not an issue, I take it, because the Prosecution put nothing forward to the -- forward before this Trial Chamber. There's no -- simply no foundation in the record for that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will respond to that. In terms of evidence, the report of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, the testimony of Marko Rajic as well as the evidence testimony of Kari Anttila. Those are just three examples of some of the witnesses who have offered evidence about the probable range of error of some of the weaponry used against Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get back because we're here primarily to hear the testimony of the witness. You put the question to him, Mr. Russo, and the witness said that certainly certain parts of town would not qualify as legitimate military targets. Let's take it from there. If you want to further explore -- first of all, apparently the witness says that there are areas which could not be legally attacked. That seemed to me a rather important starting point in the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I do agree it's important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to further explore that, please do so, perhaps not by varying your question but perhaps to put some follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, taking that as the starting point, your observation that there were certainly areas in Knin that were not legitimate military targets to fire artillery at, that's one aspect of -- of an assessment of whether -- is a difference between targeting those areas intentionally and a difference between the effects of artillery, for lack of a better term, bleeding over into those areas. You agree that there's a difference there, right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear. A lawful military objective is the only thing that a commander may deliberately make the object of attack, okay? When we use the word "target" it infers in my mind a decision by an operational leader to make something the deliberate object of attack. Only lawful military objectives within Knin could have been properly and legally targeted by General Gotovina and his subordinate commanders or staff officers. The effects of artillery do not always, we know, directly correlate to the intended target that -- that the round was fired at. So, it seems to me what you are asking and -- and if this is incorrect you can obviously tell me, is that if you know a probable range of error or a probable area of error and you could put a circle around a lawful military objective, could you conclusively infer from a round striking outside that probable range of error that the intended object of attack was not the lawful military objective. Is that an accurate -- is that what you're suggesting to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm simple trying to determine when somebody says the entire town of Knin was shelled. Shells fell everywhere over the town -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Hang on a second. Somebody says that. Now, there's, you would agree with me, only a few explanations for that. One of them being that in fact it was intended to fire shells all over the town.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I take it that you're going suggest to me that there's possibly another reason not connected to an intent, an illicit intent that would produce that kind of result. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off, again, I was told that the witness said it looked like the entire town of Knin was shelled. Your question as you just recharacterised it or rephrased it presented it as a fact. Okay? It was a perception. That is what I was told. A witness on the scene had a perception that the entire city was under attack. Yes, you are correct. If that perception is corroborated in fact or is -- or if the finder of fact, in this Tribunal I assume, concludes that based on that perception there were shells fired all over the entire city, then that would indicate an indiscriminate attack, because, as I stated earlier, there were military objectives dispersed throughout the city but that didn't make the entire city a military objective. What I said was that my reaction to that was there was an alternate rational explanation for that perception, and that alternate rational explanation is that you are observing the kinetic effect of artillery rounds that are being fired simultaneously in a coordinated effort to disrupt the enemy's ability to see the battlefield, to manoeuvre, to re-supply, to muster, and to move reinforcements. That is a fairly intense attack, each morning, around the time of twilight, where the kinetic effect of artillery is exacerbated because of the lack of natural light and the obvious flash impact of artillery, and I believe that that could create a perception that the entire city is under attack. So, yes, I think there are two alternate inferences you can draw from that perception, and that's what I explained to Defence counsel when they told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think I've got what you're putting to me. Let me just make sure if I am correct. You were, as you say, given someone's perception about what they believed they were witnessing, and you immediately stopped them and said, Well, there's two possibilities. Number one, they're right about what they saw; number two, they may be wrong and here's why. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, number one they may be right; number two, they may be wrong. And I didn't use that terminology. I said there were two rational inferences you could derive from that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It ain't necessarily so. It is not necessarily what you think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe -- Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now you also said here in connection with your second-to-last answer: "As I stated earlier, there were military objectives dispersed throughout the city but that didn't make the entire city a military objective?" Then you would agree with me, then, that if General Gotovina made the entire city a military objective of the artillery attack, that would be unlawful?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explain to me how you make an entire city the military objective? If I can ask that, with all due respect, before I answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, I think you're anticipating where I'm going with this. But I'd like you to first answer the question.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Gotovina gave an order to subordinates with the intent that that order be understood as a directive to place the entire city under attack because there were several dispersed military objectives in that city, that would have been an improper order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And as I said, I do believe you're anticipating where I'm going with this so we'll just come out with it right now. You saw the order for attack, General Gotovina's order for attack in which he directs his artillery forces to put the town of Knin under artillery fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You have also seen Brigadier Rajcic's artillery attachment in which he follows up that with an order to "shell the town of Knin." You have seen those?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you telling me that the explicit language of those orders does not indicate to you that Knin, the town of Knin was a target for artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think that that -- the language in those orders raises several possibilities. It's not language that I think is ideal by any means. If I had been a JAG officer reviewing that plan I would have gone back to the commander and I would have said, You need -- we need to revisit the terminology here. In fact, in my experience as a JAG officer, that was a routine practice, because military operators, particularly as the higher level of command you reach, you paint with a relatively broad brush, and one of the reasons why there are more than 1.800 licenced attorneys wearing uniforms in the United States Army, and more than 500 of them deployed in Afghanistan and Iraq, is a recognition that it is very common to use language in orders and directives and fragmentary orders that is not as precise as we would like it to be. So when I saw that, it obviously raised a concern in my mind, and I -- and so I considered it against broader context. There was testimony in Rajcic's transcript that talked about emphasis by General Gotovina on the propriety of targeting, that we will not make civilians the direct object of attack. There was discussion between General Gotovina and his political commander, the president, at the very outset of the Brioni transcript where the president emphasises the critical importance of maintaining international support and goodwill through the execution of the operation and uses the phrase, as I recall, We must ensure the operation is executed professionally. Now, I know that General Gotovina had experience with the French Foreign Legion prior to assuming his duties as a commander in Croatia. It -- all of this raises the question of what professional execution means if an operational commander is told by his president, We must maintain international support and ensure the operation is executed professionally, in 1995, in the Balkans, what effect does this have on his state of mind? I would assume that there had been war gaming going on. You don't execute an operation that is the strategic centre of gravity for fighting and winning a war without planning it, without war gaming it, and it's clear that military objectives within Knin were identified. It's clear that General Gotovina had a serious issue of ammunition resourcing, and a priority effort to support the tactical main effort. So all of this -- all of this, I think, goes into at least my assessment of what that would have meant and how that would have been understood, meant when it was issued, understood when it was received by subordinate commanders in the broader context of this operation. And therefore, like the perception that Knin, the entire city, is under attack, I think that in isolation, that's troubling. In broader context, there are multiple conclusions you can derive from that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It sounds, based on how you began the answer and how you ended it, you do agree that the language used by General Gotovina can admit of several possible interpretations, one of them being that in fact he did want the entire town of Knin shelled; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say, place the city under attack, then obviously one of the conclusions you can draw from that was that that was what was intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated that if you were a JAG officer reviewing this particular order you would have gone back to the commander and told him he needed to change the language, and one of the reasons you would have done that is because to follow the order explicitly would be a crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I would have done it is because I wouldn't want there to be any uncertainty as to what his intent was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just for the sake of argument, if there was, in fact, uncertainty --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we're talking about uncertainty in the order, might it not be best to pull 1125 up and deal with the actual document so we get some clarity concerning this uncertainty that counsel is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we could look at the document. At the same time, I do understand the testimony of Professor Corn to be that in order to understand exactly what was meant, that it might be not a good idea to just focus alone on that line in that order, or on those lines in those orders, that -- for the interpretation of what was meant. We have to see it in the context and then in the entirety of the evidence produced to finally form an opinion as to how to understand that order. Is that correct --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Professor Corn? Then, Mr. Kehoe, I'm not opposed against looking at the language, but it will serve only to a limited extent what you apparently seek to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what -- that's how I understood the witness. At the same time, Mr. Russo, I was already trying to find exactly where it was commented upon exactly. So look at the text as such doesn't -- doesn't harm. Might even assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness clearly know what I'm referring to. He indicates he's seen the documents. He knows the language I'm referring to. If Mr. Kehoe wants to go ahead and point out context during his redirect examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, if you understood my previous observation well, then everyone might have clear on his mind exactly the words used. I might not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly I have no objection to pulling up the order. It's P1125. I believe it's page 14 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It will be on our screen. And then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to take this a bit step by step. As long as we have it up here, we might as well read it. It indicates, bottom paragraph you see on your screen: "Group and organise the TSs and TRS-2 along the main attack axes, focus on providing artillery support to the main forces in the offensive operation through" -- and he gives several directions on how he wants that to be achieved. Number 1, providing artillery "powerful strikes against the enemy's front line. Number 2, command posts. Number 3, communication centres. Number 4, artillery firing positions. And number 5, by putting the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire. Now, would you agree with me, Professor, that the last part, number 5, taking that language as explicit, in other words, doing all of the other things I've asked to you do, firing at communication centres and artillery positions, in addition to doing those things, I want to you put the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire. You would agree with me that that explicit language is an order for an unlawful attack on the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. Because I don't think you can read it out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I asked you a very specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I -- may I finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Let me first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo. The French translation was approximately four or five lines behind, Mr. Russo. That's the reason why I tried to stop. Could you also please slow down your speed of speech. Now you can finish your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that the witness finished his answer before Mr. Russo started his next question. I think the witness was stopping because Your Honour was asking for a pause for the translation and he had further things to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked him a direct question. He gave me a direct answer. "No" was the answer to the question, that he wouldn't agree with me and that he wanted to provide an explanation. I'm going give him the opportunity to do that, but I want my questions answered first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, Correct? After you had given him some suggestions. The answer was: "No, I wouldn't agree with that." That is an answer to your question. And then the witness started to explain his question -- his answer, which is, I think, appropriate, in view of the many matters that you put to him. You started by saying, Professor Corn, because I don't think you can read it out of context, was there anything you would like to add to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Counsel asked me if I agreed that that language -- they've moved the transcript up on me, but as I recall, if I would agree with him that that language was -- called for an illegal attack or was improper, and I answered no, I wouldn't necessarily agree with you. That could be a conclusion you could derive from that language, but I think that conclusion -- but -- but when I look at it, I look at it in broader context, and in that broader context, what I see is a commander focussing his artillery, his fire support assets on tactical objectives and operational objectives. Now I think that the question you posed to me, Mr. Russo, is based on an assumption that a command post and communication centre can only exist in the town of Knin. Therefore, adding, Put Knin under attack, can only mean you want to strike objectives in Knin that you have already identified. But I read it, with my understanding as a former tactical intelligence officer, that command posts and communications centres and logistics areas exist in the close-battle area and in the rear-battle area. And then I read on in the paragraph, and again, he is focussing on the tactical effect of fire support. So, yes, I do agree with you, if the proposition is, is one possible conclusion from that language that it was an order to place the entire city under attack. That is a possible conclusion from that. I don't think that conclusion is -- or that inference is supported by the broader context of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, thank you for your answer. What I wanted to focus on was your agreement that one possible conclusion from the language is that it was in fact an order to place the entire city under attack, and I'm asking you to confirm that if that interpretation is, in fact, the correct one, then the order, this particular language issued by General Gotovina, is an order to conduct an unlawful attack on those towns.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be understood as an order to conduct an unlawful attack on those towns. Whether or not that was his intent, I think, is another question. But, yes, that is a possible conclusion you could draw from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could have P1205.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And before we move on, the interpretation you gave to the language of the order we just looked at, that it's -- you're saying it's possible, and correct me if I'm wrong, it's possible that when General Gotovina says, Fire at command posts, communication centres, artillery positions, and by putting the towns of Knin, Drvar, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire, you're saying that one interpretation is that he's attempting to communicate to his subordinates that he wants the command posts, communication centres, artillery positions inside those towns to be attacked by artillery. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. Then ...

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My point was that in the broader context of his fire support concept of operation, it is clear that the priority effort of fire support is to support the close battle. The offensive, the initiation of offensive action against an improved and established enemy defence line, and when you fight that close battle, and you're going use artillery to support it, you have to use that artillery against not just the defences but you use it against C3I and logistics that are in proximity to that close fight. It's -- it's an axiomatic principle of military operations. And so what I read that within the broader context or what I think is a possible or rational conclusion to draw from that, is that if there had been military objectives identified in Knin prior to issuing this order, he is telling his artillery subordinates, Place the objectives in Knin under attack, in support of this broader operation. He is more focussed on the objectives related to the close fight because the close fight is his priority of effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if that position you're taking is true, Professor, can you tell us why, in your view, he doesn't say, And by putting the military objectives in Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac under artillery fire? Can you explain to me what your position is on why that language, which would clarify things, certainly was not included?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, first off, for me to tell you why he didn't do it is total speculation, but can I tell you from my experience providing legal advice to military commanders, there are a number of explanations why that language would end up. First off, I doubt General Gotovina sat down and personally wrote the document. Perhaps he did. But in most cases the commander is not writing the order. The operations officer is writing the order. And the commander obviously adopts the order when he issues it under his authority, okay? He is relying on the precision of the operational officer who drafts the order. That's one factor. Another factor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. I'm trying to understand the question, and I'm also trying to understand your testimony up until now. You have testified that this language can be understood in several ways. One possible explanation being that he wanted the towns to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another one, that he intended to give orders to attack military objectives within those towns. Now, Mr. Russo, the next question to ask why would he have put it in this way is - but please correct me when my understanding is wrong - is a useless question because it all depends on how we have to understand the language. If the language intended to say, Just attack the whole of the town, then, of course, the reason why it was phrased this way, because otherwise you would have missed major parts of the town civilian parts, if he would have only attacked military objectives. If, however, on the other hand, it was intended to give an order to attack military objectives only, under those circumstances, you could say it was -- well, not -- not phrased in the best way to do that. So, therefore, the answer to your question completely depends on the interpretation to be given to this language for which Professor Corn has told us that there are several ways of doing. You could understand it A; you could understand it B. So then to ask the why, you should split that then up, to if you understand it A, why would this language be used. If you understand it B, why would that language be used? And I think, as a matter of fact, that it's so obvious that if you interpret the order as intending to attack the town as a whole, I mean, the why for the language, the answer to that question is almost given. If, however, you would interpret it in a different way, then I think in the testimony of Professor Corn we found the answer already. It's language which is not very precise, and he would have -- would he have been in a position -- he would have sent it to be reviewed. So the answers are there. The question is a useless question if you do not make a distinction between the various interpretations of the text. If you disagree with my analysis, I'd like to hear from you, and, of course, the best would be to put the questions in such a way that I'm immediately convinced of the inaccuracy of my analysis of questions and answers. But let me first ask Professor Corn, listening to the last question of Mr. Russo and listening to my analysis as why it would a useless question, would you agree or would you not agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree, and obviously the answer I started to elicit was based on an assumption that Mr. Russo is asking me if he didn't mean to put Knin under attack, why he would have used that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the alternative, I think you could ask the other question. If he meant to attack the civilian population in Knin, why didn't he say, Place the civilians in Knin under attack. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might have missed the other parts of town, Mr. Corn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which might have been ... Yes. Mr. Russo, it's close to 10.30. If you'd like to further digest my previous observations when preparing a formulation of your next question which might demonstrate that not only me but Professor Corn is wrong as well, then I'd like to give you some time for that. Apart from that, there seems to be a procedural issue to be raised by one of the parties. Therefore, I suggest, unless you would say no, one or two questions would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, just to respond to the Court's analysis. What I'm attempting to do, and it may not be clear to the Court due to my inartful phrasing of my questions, it appears to me that Mr. Corn has chosen among the possible alternatives interpretations of this and I'm attempting to test why he has chose that particular alternative, but I will find a more focussed and less useless way to ask for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, although it may be right that more time was spent on -- on an explanation which might not necessarily be the one of the Prosecution, I didn't hear Professor Corn to choose between one of these twos -- two options but we could ask him. Professor Corn, have you chosen? Do you say this is the right interpretation; that's the wrong interpretation? Or have you just said that, in the context, the interpretation by the Prosecution is not necessarily the right one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I would have to answer that by adopting the latter proposition. Now, let me just be clear. I mean, obviously in my addendum I am given facts and assumptions that focus the attack on specific military objectives in the town. So, in that regard, in relation to the addendum, I would have to say that the facts and assumptions in the addendum rebut the proposition that the Prosecution has proffered, that this was a directive to attack the entire town. Otherwise the facts and assumptions related to my assessment of each strike would be totally eviscerated. But in this specific -- with this specific question, I think there are two reasonable or rational inferences you can draw from the use of this language. I think both of them -- there are weaknesses and strengths for both of them. I just think that it needs to be read in the broader context, and I also think that if the assumption is or the assumption is he intended attack the -- to attack the town and that's why he put that language in there, then you could ask the question why wasn't he even more precise in that intent. So I think there are two rational conclusions you could draw from that language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we should have a break, Mr. Russo. Could I first ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom, Professor Corn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I was informed that there was a procedural matter to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we could go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Since we're dealing with procedural questions, Mr. Cayley, the scheduling, as it stands now, would not permit the Cermak Defence to start its case on the 17th of September. Therefore, that date has to be changed. Now I do remember that, at the time, you asked for a couple of days between the Gotovina case and the start of the Cermak case. Now, there are two possible explanations of this language. The one being that you needed a couple of days between the two; or that you felt that, in view of the scheduling at that time, well, the 14th or the 15th would be too early and that you would need, in more absolute terms, until a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you, Mr. President, because I can short-circuit this. We are ready to actually go ahead immediately, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- as soon as the Gotovina team is finished, we can proceed with our first witness. All we need is a date for certain when our case is to begin so that we can bring our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say that could be the day after the Gotovina Defence has concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, I think we have in -- in view of the witnesses we have on our list and the estimates of time needed, we would know when that would be, but perhaps you verify and if the parties agree when the Gotovina Defence will conclude its case presentation that we will know that the next day you would start, and then we can check whether your understanding of when the Gotovina case concludes is the same as our understanding of when that will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will follow up on that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will have a break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, the Presiding Judge put the question to you, whether you had chosen between the interpretations to be given to the particular language about putting the towns under artillery fire, and you indicated that you had chosen an interpretation and your interpretation was that this was a legitimate order not intended to specifically target the town as such. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to the Judge that when I wrote my addendum, which was an assessment of the legality of placing certain targets within Knin under attack, then obviously the facts and assumptions upon which that addendum -- those -- that opinion or those opinions are premised by implication, I think, has to adopt the conclusion that this order meant, Place the objectives in Knin under attack, because that's what the facts and assumptions that drove that addendum indicated. I also told the Judge that looking at this document in and of itself, I think it is inconclusive which interpretation is -- whether one interpretation is so clear that it rules out, as a fair and rational alternative, the other interpretation. I think that -- that you could draw a logical inference that either interpretation is appropriate. I do think that -- that in context the interpretation that it was an indication to strike military objectives is a little bit weightier, but I'm not saying that it is a conclusive determination on my part, looking at that document, in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, looking at the document, not just in and of itself but in the context of everything you have already been told about the case, the facts and assumptions you were asked to rely upon, everything essentially that you are aware of up to this point, looking at that order now, can you offer an opinion to the Trial Chamber about what your interpretation of that is?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, my -- my opinion is that that was not a directive to engage in an indiscriminate attack against Knin. In my opinion, in the broader context of the commander's operational intent, his priority of effort, the tactical emphasis throughout the rest of the document, the information he was provided by the president, the emphasis on professional operations, his background as a professional soldier and non-commissioned officer in one of the most professional military organisations in the world, all of this -- and candidly, another factor that -- that weighed -- that leads me to that opinion is that because it appears to me that his focus is -- he has got a very clear battle focus, close with and destroy the enemy. Unsurprising to me from a commander who finds his lineage in a light infantry elite unit, because that is the ethos of light infantry; close with and destroy the enemy. And that -- that focus kind of, for me, seems apparent through the vast majority of information I've seen. And so, I also think that in the broader context it would be a waste of resources when he has made it clear that his priority effort is to bring the enemy armed forces into submission, to waste this fairly precious asset, his indirect fire capability, on random kind of chaotic strikes against the city. So all of that combined led me to the opinion that this was not an intent or a directive to place the city under attack or -- at large, but to strike the pre-established and identified military objectives within the city under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit D970. I believe that's -- yes, that is the one on the screen. If we can go to page 3 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, this is a copy of the attachment for artillery to General Gotovina's offensive operation order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if could move the screen a little bit further down on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Under subsection 3, the TRS task, and focussing on the language in the paragraph that says: "Shell the towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac." Do you take the same interpretation of this language as you have of General Gotovina's language in the offensive operation order.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And I think there's another element here that needs -- that I need to explain why I conclude ... Listen, I have done this process where you receive an operations order from higher command and then you produce your order in response to that. This is -- now, I have never done it in combat, right? I have done it in training and I have been involved in the process in training extensively. And even in a training environment the pressure of time, of intensity, of the -- the multiple demands that are on the staff, result in the logical process of lifting language from the superior's order and plugging it into yours. And just like I have doubts that General Gotovina actually sat down and typed his operations order, as opposed to giving his concept of operation and commander's intent and leaving it to his staff to put that into writing, I think the same process happens at the subordinate command level. A staff officer is preparing this order, he is trying to do as efficiently and timely as possible, and he is lifting stuff out of the higher command's order. But, again, you see that the general tone of the tasks to the artillery unit are tactical, okay?
