They're talking about protecting flanks, counter-battery fires, neutralising or disrupting the ability of the enemy to bring resupply and reinforcements into the main battle area, and then the language comes right out of the higher headquarters order, Shell the towns of Drvar, Knin and the rest. So, again, I think it's inartful. It leads to multiple possible interpretations. It's not language, I think, that would be in any sense ideal to place in an operations order. I think a JAG officer reviewing it would have -- would have required the staff officer writing it to make it more precise. But I think that in broader context I can understand how it ends up in -- in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Professor, with respect to General Gotovina's offensive operation order you indicated that if that you had seen that order, you would have taken it back to the commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is it the same situation applying to this particular order?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you agree that it is inartful and subject to multiple interpretations, and again, one of those interpretations is in fact -- or could be reasonably understood to be that whoever drafted this order wanted the entire towns of Drvar, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac to be shelled. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think -- I don't see how that couldn't be an interpretation. So, yes, I think that could be an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you took significant exception to what you, I believe, termed as "inartful language" used in -- in Professor Konings's [sic] report on statements of the law. Wouldn't you agree that this is slightly more of a serious matter to be so inartful when you're directing artillery to be used in a civilian-populated area?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, as I noted to the Tribunal, I am sympathetic to what Colonel Konings did with regard to the law and I spent -- I think I spent a good bit of time talking about what I saw was a conflation between policy and law; but I also said I thought it was totally understandable, because of my experience advising officers in positions similar to Colonel Konings. So what I took -- I think the characterisation of the exception that I took to his report focussed more on what I saw were modifications or distortions of operational doctrine, which I actually remember pointing to the record and saying, That's what I said was inexplicable. So if you recall, I said the confusion between RoE and law I felt was explicable. It was misleading but it was explicable. And that is consistent with my reaction to this. As a JAG officer who has been trained in the Law of Armed Conflict and support to military operations, when I receive an order, the first annex I turn to is the fire support annex, because I know how likely it is that operators in -- under the stress of -- of military operations and the requirements to do a hundred things when they have time to do 20 things, I know the proclivity to make these kind of statements. And so that, as I said, is why if you are in a military that has the luxury of having a robust legal corps, that corps is fully employed. But -- so when you -- when you ask, is this just as dangerous as Colonel Konings's imprecision in his discussion of law, there is certainly danger here. But what you have to understand this is -- this is a trigger, okay? It triggers application of targeting annexes, pre-planned targets, targets of opportunity, a whole range of process is triggered by the order to execute a mission. This doesn't stand on its own. And so in the broader context of a subordinate command where the emphasis has been placed on the tactical reduction of enemy capability, that would offset the risk, and the more of emphasis there has been on that, the greater the risk is offset as a result of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you would agree with me that however the process ran, whether General Gotovina sat down and typed this out, whether Brigadier Rajcic typed it out or somebody else typed it out, the ultimate responsibility for the language used and for the intent expressed by the language is General Gotovina's responsibility. You would agree with me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's his order. He is accountable for what it includes. But again, if you refer back to my initial report, there is a principle of IHL, I believe, that allows commanders to rely on the expectation that subordinates will interpret their orders consistent with their legal obligations. So yes. The answer to your question is yes, he is ultimately responsible for this. And if this is all there was, that would raise a significant concern. But in a broader context, I think that ultimate responsibility has to be assessed within that broader context, which I assume is the purpose of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Getting back to some of the questions I was asking you earlier, there was one I neglected to ask regarding what you were told during your oral presentation in December of 2008. Were you told about or shown any evidence in relation to the shelling conducted by General Gotovina's forces in any areas other than Knin during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Professor, have you ever spoken with General Gotovina or any of his former subordinate officers in the HV?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never spoken to General Gotovina. I mentioned that there was a technical expert that was in the meeting in Tampa, a gentleman named Goran. I apologise to the Tribunal; I don't know his last name. I believe he was in the HV armed forces. I have -- I don't think, to my knowledge, he was part of General Gotovina's staff. But that's the only individual that I have had contact with that I think had experience as an HV -- a member of the HV armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, since you are revisiting the presence of persons during the Tampa -- yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't know if you're -- by -- in transparency, the individual is Goran Zugic, Z-u-g-i-c, the gentleman who has been in court from time to time, has been a part of our team. I just wanted to make that clear and so the Prosecution knows who this individual is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Russo. Early, Mr. Corn, you referred to the three counsel that are in court. Well, on our filings we find three counsel, two of them are in court at this moment. So it was not entirely clear what -- to which person you referred when you were talking about a third counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lawyers that were in the meeting were Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Stanton and Mr. Cronin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this gentleman Goran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, have you, on your own, been exposed to any information about this case, either through media, law review articles, watching testimony, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before this, I wasn't familiar with General Gotovina. As a matter of fact, the night -- the day arrived here, I pulled up a Wikipedia site just so I could see a picture of what he looked like. That was the first time I saw a picture of the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge or information concerning the conflict in Croatia, concerning specifically Operation Storm itself?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any specific information related to Operation Storm. As an army Judge Advocate at the time, I was generally familiar that there was a conflict going on between the Croatians and the Croatian Serbs. But the specific details of the conflict I was unfamiliar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, have you ever been to Knin?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Have you ever been to anywhere else in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have been to Dubrovnik, but I don't think that is in the Krajina so ... that's only the place in Dubrovnik -- or in Croatia I've visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you have any contact with any member of any Defence team other than General Gotovina's Defence team in relation to this case?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, at paragraph 13 of your supplemental information sheet, that's D1644, you state: "I reviewed these documents" -- and that's referring to the documents listed in paragraph 12, "within the scope of my conclusions, as stated in paragraph 11. To the extent these documents were relevant to that scope, none of them changed my conclusions." Professor, I had a little difficulty understanding what you were trying to convey about the limitations on your conclusions in paragraph 11 and here again in paragraph 13 of your supplemental information sheet. Can you please just give us an explanation of this.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. You know, obviously I wrote the addendum prior to preparing to be a witness. The preparation for being a witness, as I testified to yesterday, involved ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Involved the visit to Houston by Mr. Cronin and Mr. Stanton in which we reviewed my addendum and other information; for example, the Brioni transcript, some of the orders we've just looked at. It also involved a meeting here in The Hague at the offices of Greenberg Traurig, which we conducted Sunday, and I signed this document that day. And the point that is made by that paragraph is subsequent to writing the addendum, I haven't seen any document that has called -- that would lead me to change the opinions in that addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can I take it that that means you conducted a thorough review of the documents which are listed in paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't use the characterisation thorough. I have seen these documents or photographs. I think I've indicated to you the ones that I thought had a significant impact on my thought process. Others had an -- obviously a less significant impact, so it's -- you're -- it would depend what your meaning of "thorough" is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, to say, I have looked at these documents and they haven't changed my conclusions, I'm taking that to mean that you took an intellectually honest review of those to -- you know, because if there is something in there that may have changed your opinion and you missed it because you didn't give it a thorough enough reading --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- that is something we might want to consider.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And I think my point is that there are some that I felt were not that significant. Others that I felt were more significant. And the ones that triggered my sense that they were more significant led to a more intense review. For example, when I read the order and it says put the cities of or the towns of blank, blank, blank under attack, it's a red flag and I'm going to spend more time looking at or -- maybe thinking about that context. But, no, it's not as if somebody stuck a paper in front of me and said, Check it off, or a photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in your expert report, that last full paragraph on page 28, you state: "The record indicates that General Gotovina appears to have considered these aspects of the disposition of civilians in Knin when selecting his course of action for employing his indirect fire assets. My review of the record indicates the following with relation to the actual employment of indirect fires by General Gotovina." Now, the record you are referring to there means the facts and assumptions specifically provided to you by the Gotovina Defence in the May 19th letter; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in fact, the items of information which you identify on pages 28 and 29 as relevant to General Gotovina's use of artillery, they're copied verbatim from the assumed facts provided on pages 6 and 7 of the Gotovina Defence's May 19th letter to you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find the letter before I ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in identifying pieces of information that you considered relevant, there was no other piece of information you believe was worth mentioning regarding General Gotovina's use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me, once again, reiterate the process that drove this. I was being asked to opine on what I considered to be the ultimate question before the Tribunal: Was the General's employment of artillery consistent with his obligations under the Law of Armed Conflict? I went to the Defence and I said -- their initial offer to me was to give me documents and transcripts, et cetera, et cetera. I told them I thought that what was important was that my opinion be based on a factual predicate that was consistent with the factual record at the trial. That's probably why I used the word "record." It would have been more precise for me to say, Based on the facts and assumptions provided. But I was, I guess, kind of subconsciously associating those facts and assumptions with the record because I had insisted on several occasions that the Defence give me their assurance that they were confident that the record supported these facts and assumptions. And that's why I attempted to rely on them to render my opinion, because if I create or use other facts and assumptions that are not before the Tribunal, in my opinion, when I wrote this, the value of my opinion is degraded. Because all can I understand that I'm doing is offering my insight, based on my expertise, to aid the finder of fact reaching the ultimate conclusion, and the value of that assistance is, in my view, directly connected to the factual foundation upon which it rests. And the only thing, the only fact that I thought was particularly significant that I went to them and said, I remember this, and if it is before the Tribunal, I think it's significant, was the decision to refrain from launching an attack on co-mingled civilian and military individuals fleeing out of the -- the incursion area. So that's the best explanation I can give you, as to why I can find the opinion to the foundation established by the facts and assumptions offered in the letter, or attempted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, when you listed the information here, by this time you had already seen General Gotovina's offensive operation order which you've already indicated raised a red flag for you. And in listing the information you believed was relevant to his use of artillery you didn't think it was a fact worth mentioning that he used the language which raised a red flag in your mind? You didn't think that was something that the Trial Chamber should know was part of your consideration?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I explained to you, okay, in the abstract that concerned me. In the broader context, I think I understood what it meant. That was my opinion. Okay? And so -- the answer is no. I mean, obviously if I had thought that was important to add to the facts and assumptions, I would have asked the Defence counsel if I could include it, like the fact of deciding not to fire on those fleeing forces. It is a -- I felt the -- the tactical execution, the overall situation, and the facts related to the effects of fires was more significant in my assessment, because it put it into broader context. Honestly, I can't even -- I can't even remember if I thought to myself, That's already before the Tribunal. They'll -- obviously they'll be considering that. I don't even remember if I went through that thought process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, before we look at some of the assumed facts which you identify as relevant to your considerations, let me ask you this: Would you agree with me that at times when you had no information on particular factual circumstances you made assumptions or inferences favourable to General Gotovina to fill in that informational gap? Would you concede that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me a specific example of where you think I did that? I mean, are you taking in relation to these facts and assumptions or ... When I first -- when I first began the case, I had -- I had no opinion one way or the other as to whether he acted properly. My first function was to look at a report written by Colonel Konings and help the Defence counsel identify what I thought were problems with the report, the case progressed from there. So I don't think at every point I had an assumption that General Gotovina was acting properly and I filled in facts and circumstances to -- to bolster that assumption. And by the way, in that regard, as I said yesterday, if the Trial Chamber determines that this factual predicate is erroneous and another factual predicate substitutes for it, then I recognise that many of the opinions in here are invalidated. So, ultimately, there's a -- the critical question is: What were the facts and circumstances and assumptions related to the decision-making process at the time he made the decision, which is emphasised in my first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Looking at your report at the top of page 28, specifically looking at subsection (b), you point out the assumption provided to you that there was a curfew imposed against civilians. And if we move to the next page and look at the bottom where you draw some conclusions based on those facts, at subsection A you conclude that General Gotovina: "... sought to exploit the curfew by surging his indirect fires against military objectives in Knin during curfew hours." Further down in subsection (c), you conclude that General Gotovina: "... employed indirect fires during non-curfew hours in a limited manner, suggesting an intent to disrupt enemy operations while minimizing the risk of collateral damage and incidental injury to civilians." And finally on the following page, that's page 30, in subsection (f), you conclude that General Gotovina: "... employed MBRLs only during those times he assumed civilians were under a curfew order." Now, Professor, when you drafted this addendum, at least according to the testimony you have given us, you didn't actually have any evidence concerning what the curfew hours were, and looking through the assumed facts that you identified as relevant, as well as all of the assumed facts which you were asked to assume by the Gotovina Defence, there is no indication of what the curfew hours actually were. So what I'm putting to you is that you made a determination without knowing what the curfew hours were, what General Gotovina's conduct was and intent was, relative to those curfew hours. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only explanation is that I was aware that the curfew was through, I believe, 5.00 in the morning. So -- and as I told you yesterday, I don't think it was -- I couldn't say that when I wrote this addendum I expunged every bit of information that I'd ever heard. So my answer to your question is, obviously when I put that down I was referring to knowledge that I had learned probably in the meeting in Tampa, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, without getting into what you learned at Tampa, you learned because you were provided with documentation --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Specifically if we could have Exhibit D241.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You were provided with the document I am about to show you which indicates that, in fact, what you say here about the curfew hours is wrong. That it -- in fact the situation is opposite from what you conclude. Your conclusions that General Gotovina surged his indirect fires during curfew hours, you'll see from the document, is incorrect. It indicates that the curfew is from 10.00 p.m. to 5.00 a.m. As you may know, it is undisputed in this case that 5.00 a.m. is the time when General Gotovina chose to begin and in fact did begin his artillery attack. And so, in fact, it was during non-curfew hours --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- that he surged his artillery. So now that you know the situation is the opposite of what you thought it was when you drew this conclusion, are you willing to draw the opposite conclusion? Knowing now that he surged his artillery and used his artillery during non-curfew hours, does that suggest to you an intent, in fact, to increase the risk to civilians?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. Now, first off, let me make the point. I mean, this is an example of the point I just made in response to your earlier question. I recognise that if the -- if the record, the facts determined by the Chamber, the Trial Chamber, are inconsistent with the facts and assumptions that I base my report on, then the value of the opinion is degraded as a result of that. Now, the level of degradation is something that the Trial Chamber assesses. In this situation, I believe that, based on the overall record, his use of indirect fires against the C3I targets in Knin, the surge of indirect fires was driven primarily by his consideration of the connection to the tactical point of attack. In other words, if you're launching your attack at twilight, it doesn't make sense to launch your assault on the CP at midnight because within the six or seven hours between midnight and twilight, the enemy has freedom of action. It -- it's -- I obviously remember that there was a curfew in and around that time. Now, if you tell me that the surge of artillery occurred at noon, or 2.00 in the afternoon, and it is unrelated to the launching of the offensive operation and it's so attenuated from the termination of the curfew that it creates a high probability that there are going to be civilians out and about, then that, I think, would have a much more significant degrading effect on the opinion. But you're talking about the difference between 5.00 and 5.30, suggesting -- I mean, I don't think it's a rational inference that at 5.00 in the morning when the curfew ends, everybody jumps up and runs outside. Now maybe that is true, and maybe I don't know the cultural dynamics of people who lived in Knin, and if that's established then the opinion loses significant weight. I fully concede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Professor. However, the point I'm making, which I believe you have made for me, is you don't know what was going on at 5.00 a.m. --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- you're making an assumption when do you that, that they're not walking through the streets at 5.00 a.m., they're not out in their fields, they're not feeding their animals, and that is an assumption which is favourable to General Gotovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I mean, I -- the context of that question, with all due respect, has got to have some foundation in the record, and I ask, if in fact that's a question to be levelled, that counsel should point to where in the record, at 5.00 a.m., people were walking the streets of Knin, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo is exploring the underlying rationale for the conclusions drawn. He puts to the witness that one of the assumptions he used is not necessarily correct; the curfew hours being until 5.00. And then you can explore, because we're talking about the abstract, the witness doesn't know whether the curfew hours were strictly observed. The witness doesn't know a lot of these things. To that extent, we are already in an area of assumptions. I'll not use the word "speculations." Under those circumstances, if the witness explains to us that it's not necessarily true that if the curfew ends at 5.00, that everyone immediately moves on the streets, and it would be different if we would be talking about 2.00 in the afternoon. I would ask the witness whether, if people would be used to get up at 4.00 and do their things, whether it could well be - I'm not saying it was - that people, already delayed for one hour, would do that immediately at 5.00 in the morning. I mean, that's not of any less logic than to say that people would not immediately jump out at 5.00. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With one qualifier, Your Honour, and that is, if that was the expectation of the commander making the decision. If he had information that, because people normally begin their day at 4.00, the curfew to 5.00 has them ready to go at 5.00. Then yes, that significantly undermines the value of the assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I understand a bit of the explanation you gave me earlier about the use of artillery relative to the curfew hours. But the point I'm trying to make is that you made a statement in your expert report that said because General Gotovina employed indirect fires during non-curfew hours in a limited manner, suggesting an intent to disrupt enemy operations while minimising the risk of collateral damage and incidental injury to civilians, you're the one who made the connection between the curfew hours and the risk to civilians.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And when I'm telling that you the document that I'm now showing you, in fact, changes that situation, why are you not now willing to change the inference you drew when you had the wrong information?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are three answers to that. First off, you see in subparagraph (c), I used the words "suggesting an intent." It's just an inference. That's all it is. There may be an alternative inference. I think if he is surging his fires in the -- in the -- against the military objectives in the populated area at a time where he believes, where he believes, he can exploit the effect of the curfew and still achieve his -- his operational purpose, then that -- those two factors are relevant. And if you look at (b), the primary emphasis is on his employment of indirect fires consistent with METT-T-C analysis, which is corroborated by the fact that the majority of the assets were not employed against assets in Knin, but instead associated -- targets associated with the close fight and enemy defensive positions. I don't think -- okay, this is my opinion. If he knew the curfew ended at 3.00 a.m. but that the main effort was going to begin at 5.00 a.m., I think he would have still surged his artillery at 5.00 a.m., because I believe the use of the artillery in Knin was -- was synchronised or connected with the purpose of the overall employment of indirect fire, which was to defeat the enemy at the point of attack as efficiently as possible. All I was suggesting there is that if he believed that there was a positive effect from the curfew, then it would have been another factor that would have supported the inference that his decision to surge at that time was a reasonable decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Professor, before reaching this conclusion, you weren't actually provided with any evidence from the Gotovina Defence about what General Gotovina believed was going on in the town at 5.00 a.m. At least we don't see it represented anywhere. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, you weren't provided --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was provided with what -- I don't have any -- I didn't get any statements, you know, confessions, statements, testimony from General Gotovina. I don't know what was exactly in his mind at that time. And if you look at my original report, I emphasise the fact that when assessing -- when translating a -- a Law of Armed Conflict principle that's -- was written and intended to provide an operational decision-making framework into criminal responsibility, a standard of criminal responsibility, one of the great challenges is figuring out what was the defendant's state of mind, and that oftentimes you have to rely on the circumstantial evidence to do that. I fully acknowledge and recognise that that is the challenge that confronts this Tribunal or any Tribunal assessing an allegation of criminality based on a violation of rules of targeting. And those -- that's what I attempted to do in my opinion, based on the facts and circumstances that were provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 2161.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, this is a report by the HV intelligence administration dated 30 July 1995. And if we can look at page 2 in the English, and it's page 1 in the B/C/S, middle of the second paragraph on page 2, it states: "In addition to issuing the decision to engage all human and material resources in the defence of the RSK, the military council imposed a curfew (between 2200 and 5000 hours)." Now, Professor, in line with what you just said about the necessity of considering circumstantial evidence, would you agree that this is something that -- a piece of information that General Gotovina must have taken into account when deciding when exactly to begin his artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't know if the witness has ever seen this document before. I don't suspect that he has. If he is given the opportunity to look at the document, I think it is only fair of witness, to allow him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, Professor Corn, I take it that if you see a document you would like to have a closer look at because you're unfamiliar with it, that you will address me. Now, Mr. Kehoe was kind enough to -- to make this observation. Is there any need you'd like to like at the document any further at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I see the beginning of it so I could see where it -- what its origin was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo told you already it's a report by the HV intelligence administration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dated 30th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm ready, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Would you agree, Professor, that this is information that General Gotovina was required to take into consideration before deciding when exactly to begin his artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the C in METT-T-C analysis. A competent and -- a competent commander, if he has this information available, should be made aware of it, probably through his intelligence officer or his civil affairs officer, in the target decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can I take that as a yes?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, you used the phrase -- and I don't -- let's see, "is required," I think you said, right? I have trouble with "is required." Okay? He should be made aware of it. He should be aware of it. The required part, is a commander required to be aware of every bit of information that his intelligence officer receives? Well, that's impossible. That's why he has an intelligence officer, because the intelligence officer, based on his priority intelligence requirements, distills this volume of information and provides him relevant information related to operations. I think this is relevant related to the use of indirect fire in a populated area. So I would have expected his intelligence officer to make him aware of this information. But if his intelligence officer did not, then the nature of your question suggests that the General is ipso facto culpable for not knowing it. He relies on his staff to provide him information. And I can only correlate it to my own experience. This report, in my experience, would not have gone directly to the General. It would have gone to his intelligence staff, and they would have distilled it and then provided him the information they thought was necessary. It -- it's the reality of a commander executing -- planning and executing a battle. He is inundated with information and challenges and responsibilities and that's why commanders employ staffs, to aid them in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It is General Gotovina's responsibility to keep himself informed on concentrations of civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to have 65 ter 2161 admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2619.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2619 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, in section 1 of your addendum - and that appears at page 25 of your report - you discuss the targeting process and the need to select the appropriate weapon to achieve the desired effect on targets. In the second-to-last full paragraph you state: "Based on my review of General Gotovina's operational situation, it seems clear that his options for asset selection were limited. There is no indication he possessed a robust electronic warfare capability for a disruption mission, nor did he possess the type of precision engagement capability increasingly associated with counter-C3I operations conducted by advanced Western militaries, like the United States. Instead, his capability was essentially limited to indirect fire assets, ground combat assets and a very limited rotary-air capability." Professor, in pointing out that you saw no indication that General Gotovina possessed a "robust electronic warfare capability," I take it that you considered that as a relevant factor in your analysis of whether General Gotovina's choice of weaponry was reasonable under the circumstances; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly a factor in the targeting process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And having found no indication of a robust electronic warfare capability, did you ask the Gotovina Defence to provide you with information relating to the HV's electronic warfare capabilities?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know had -- I know I asked that question in Tampa, okay? I specifically asked what were the EW assets. As a former intelligence officer that was one of my functions, was to have expertise on electronic warfare and provide that -- the knowledge of that capability in the targeting and weaponeering process. So I was curious as to whether or not the HV had the type of robust electronic warfare units that the United States had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, what were you told in response to the question?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- as best I recall, I seem to recall some discussion of maybe one helicopter that had a jamming capability, but I think, as I recall, that was it. But certainly not a communications and electronic warfare battalion like you would find in a United States corps. And, you know, part of it was me learning what these designations were for the HV. I mean, when I initially began to look at this and I see corps, right, Croatian corps or a Serbian corps, that triggers an instinct on my part about, you know, what an American corps looks like. And in fact, I think that I came out of this realizing that what they call a corps is what we call maybe a brigade combat team, a much smaller unit with a much less significant support structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, electronic warfare capabilities would include, as you mentioned, radio jamming. Would they also include radio deception and use of electronic surveillance?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- it's been a long time since I have looked at military intelligence doctrine, but my recollection is deception falls under a different category than electronic warfare. Electronic warfare, as I recall -- certainly as I think of it, involves direction finding, electronic equipment that triangulates transmission for precision targeting. Jamming, interception, right, so you can listen to what the enemy is saying. And destruction. There are some electronic warfare assets that can actually burn up enemy transmitters. So transmission capability. All right, the ability to transmit a false radio report I wouldn't normally put in the category of electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 2156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting, perhaps you could tell us in what category that would fit, if it's not electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the capability to transmit is communications. And the use of that transmission to put out false information is deception. And the reason that I -- I think instinctually I see them as different assets is because, in my experience, doctrinally, electronic warfare falls under the responsibility of the intelligence officer. As a matter of fact, in -- in the US military, the commander of electronic warfare units is an intelligence officer. It's one of the few command billets for an intelligence officer. Deception falls under the responsibility of the operations officer. And so you could use a piece of communications equipment, you could use a piece of electronic warfare equipment to -- to create deception, to communicate a deceptive message. But I don't see the deception operation as within the category of electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, electronic warfare being the assets that were used rather than for what they were used. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think, with all due respect, Your Honour, I guess I confused it, the opposite. As a matter of fact, there's an acronym in the US military called MIJI, meaconing, interception, jamming, and interference. And that's kind of when you're in an operation and every tactical standing operating procedure has a report that a subordinate command is supposed to send up when he feels he has been the victim of enemy electronic warfare, and it is called a MIJI report; meaconing, interception, jamming, and interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, on the screen we have a 31 July 1995 request from the chief of HV intelligence administration to General Gotovina for approval to conduct "electronic warfare and radio deception," in the Split Military District. You can have a look at this. It's not very long.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can I take it that this is a document that you had not seen before and something that you had not considered when you made the determination that General Gotovina did not possess a robust electronic warfare capability?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen this. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I move for the admission of 65 ter 2156.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 7146.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: On the screen, Professor, we have HV plan of electronic surveillance and jamming, dated 1 August 1995. You can see this will -- one of the later pages, it includes Gotovina's -- General Gotovina's approval of a plan for electronic detection, monitoring and jamming.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 in the English and also page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. President, if the witness can take a look at this document from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, as a matter of fact, that I invited the witness that if he wants to look at something that he'll address me. I take it that you understood this invitation. If there's any need, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to just scan it from the beginning, Your Honour, before we jump to page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, could you ... yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, if we could go back to that page, page 7 is the one I wanted to look at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You can see at the top left-hand corner approval by General Gotovina. And you can see the tasks -- the mode of tasks which are given, detecting and monitoring, detect and monitor radio communications between the VRSK, Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, 15th Corps, and TK, and radio communications between the VRS, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next one, please. Or the bottom of that one. Could I see the bottom of the last page? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, again, this is not a document that you considered before determining whether General Gotovina possessed a robust electronic warfare capability; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, I'm not correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't consider this. This is the first time I have seen this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I move for the admission of 65 ter 7146.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2621 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can please have 65 ter 7351 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I make a comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The entire task of subordinate units is a monitoring tasks. You can monitor with your own radios. Monitor means listen to enemy transmission. Disruption of enemy transmissions requires jamming capability. Now, you can use your own radio, theoretically, to jam. If I get on your frequency and tape my mic down, and make a hot mic, you're going hear static on your frequency until I stop doing it, or until you change your channel, okay? But this suggests to me two things. First of, again, a total operational focus for the collection effort. And, second, he is not giving a directive to jam in this report. Now maybe there is another one but he's telling people to monitor, Gather as much information as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 7351, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you have on your screen an order from the chief of the HV main staff, General Cervenko, on electronic warfare dated 30 July 1995 for "efficient use of UHF jamming device and for the purpose of carrying out electronic fight during the HV attack in a unique way." And he directs the formation of electronic warfare units. You can see - if we move down a bit - on the left-hand side, the 4th Guards Brigade gets one jamming station for its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we move to the next page in English but stay on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Towards the top, the 5th Guards Brigade gets also one jamming station. But you will note that the 7th Guards Brigade electronic warfare platoon, whose area of responsibility includes Knin, gets two jamming stations. Now, Professor, this again is a document that you did not consider. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I move for the admission of 65 ter 7351.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2622.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2622 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please have Exhibit D965, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, what we have on the screen right now is an HV plan of intelligence support, dated 2 August 1995. It is directing the use of electronic reconnaissance units for gathering intelligence on enemy composition and disposition. You will note at the top left-hand corner approval on behalf of General Gotovina. Just take a look at the some of the entries. It indicates gathering intelligence on the enemy strength, disposition, and organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You will note the tasks all for the most part relate to collecting information, detecting enemy movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, gathering information on locations of command posts, disposition tasks, possible directions of attack of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: More tasks with respect to collecting information about the enemy, possible combat dispositions. Also monitoring enemy losses in manpower and technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, taking note of the directions given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. If we could move back one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you can see from what we've looked at, this plan of intelligence report, there were no orders to use electronic means for collecting information about the civilian population. You would agree with me that that's something that can also be done with -- by using electronic means; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, as I say, it's been a long time since I have written an intelligence annex to an operations order. In our practice, gathering information about the civilian population is the function of the S5 or the S6, the civil affairs staff officer in the command who is part of the targeting process. Now whether or not the civil affairs officer is going to suggest to the operations officer and the intelligence officer to make that collection mission a -- a mission for electronic warfare or electronic meaconing assets, I don't know. I do know this. That looking at this, there's -- there's a clear connection between what I -- what we would call the -- the commander's mission essential task list, which is defeat the enemy in depth, prevent the enemy from massing and reinforcing, and isolate enemy positions at the front line, and the task to electronic assets. So I -- clearly there is no task in there to monitor civilian activity. But I don't know that a listening station is necessarily an ideal asset to obtain that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thanks, Professor. I'm not asking to you draw any conclusions from the fact that there is no direction to collect information on the civilian population. I just wanted your confirmation that that is a function to which these assets could be put.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming there was something to intercept that would reveal the disposition or movement of civilian assets, then yes, you could use an intercept asset for that purpose. But I think that you have -- it's just like artillery. You have a limited number of assets, and you have a -- and you have a range of probability of gaining good information so you -- you focus those limited assets where you can get the best information. If there was evidence that, for example, I don't know, that there was a convoy that was evacuating a group of civilians and that the -- the intelligence staff knew the convoy was using VHF or UHF communications, to notify maybe a UN headquarters of its movement, I don't know. Then theoretically you would say that could be a good way of finding out where the convoy is. But there are -- I guess what I'm saying is there are multiple factors that would go into whether or not you would task your electronic assets for that purposes. In the right circumstances, you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can I take it that the document on the screen is not one that you considered?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, that you've seen some evidence at least of electronic warfare compatibilities at General Gotovina's disposal, would you agree that if you had time to consider these things in the context of everything else you have learned, that it could possibly have an effect on the conclusions that you reached?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it could have. Although, from what I've seen, it wouldn't have -- I don't think it would have significantly altered the opinion. And, I mean, if you want me to tell you why, I will; if not, I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, if you have already made a determination about that, I will certainly hear that from you.

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First off, you have to understand what jamming assets are and what they do, and -- and -- and that plays into the effects based targeting. A jamming asset is no different than a kinetic artillery round. It's an asset at the commander's disposal that produces an effect. But it's got some drawbacks. To jam somebody you have to discharge a high frequency, high-power frequency, over the enemy's frequency. The enemy anticipates jamming and that's why the enemy, just like friendly forces, will have redundant communication systems and plans for channel skipping. In other words, if you pick up your radio and you're jammed, you have a default next frequency to move to. The other risk with jamming is you -- if your enemy has direction finding capability, jamming presents a high-value target for the enemy, because that high-intensity frequency that you're discharging is easily triangulated. And therefore, if have you limited jamming assets, you have to use them judiciously, and you have to use them at the right time for the right time. The discussion of electronic warfare, in my opinion, related to the artillery attack on the corps headquarters, a critical C3I target, and other targets that had the capability of providing redundant communications to the enemy. And if you had jammed, you would have achieved an effect maybe for a certain period of time. Your jamming asset would have been highly vulnerable to counter-attack, and the enemy has ways of -- of mitigating the effect of that jamming. And the other thing is, if you -- if you look at this order, you see that the commander is planning an operation in depth, and we -- I talked yesterday about this full spectrum dominance idea, right? You disable the commander, the corps commander's C3I capability. You blind the corps commander and the corps commander's staff, it degrades that commander's ability to influence the fight by logistics reinforcement and direction. But if you isolate the forces at the tip of the spear, if you make them feel they can't talk to anybody, then you increase their sense of isolation and that increases your initiative. So it's conceivable that with limited jamming assets the priority of effort to support the ground tactical assault would have led the commander to make a reasonable judgement that, I'm going use my jamming assets to blind the forward command posts and an alternative asset to degrade the rear command posts. It just -- that's why throughout that report you see that term "METT-T-C." It goes into the decision to use every asset within the commander's arsenal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, you injected the term "limited jamming assets." I'm trying to found out where -- I mean, I understand you were told --

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: -- that he had limited assets. I have now shown you some evidence of assets he did have at his disposal. Do you still consider those assets to be limited?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I'm basing it on my own contextual experience, which is a brigade combat would have an entire battalion or at least a company of electronic warfare capability which would have more than two or three jammers, and you do that because you know those jammers are tremendously vulnerable to counter-attack once you put them into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: But the effectiveness of your jamming capabilities and, of course, how many people you have, whether you have a platoon, you have a brigade, whatever, that's all relative to the size of the enemy you're fighting, the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's also -- absolutely. That -- there is no question about that. That is the E in METT-T-C. Right? But it is also contingent on communications redundancy, how many nets the enemy has. You see by the monitoring annex that he is focussing on multiple enemy communications networks. So, for example, when I was an intelligence officer in a light infantry unit I carried a radio, an encrypted radio, on my back. When the commander's radio was jammed, he would walk over to me and he'd pick up my radio, and he would give command through the intelligence net. And if that was jammed, he would give it through the logistics net. So there are multiple nets. So if you only have -- if you're trying to blind the commander's command and control function and you're going to use jammers exclusively, you have to make sure have you enough jammers to deny or degrade not only the command net but all redundant communications capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, looking at some of the information I have shown you, would you agree that this is information relevant to the consideration of the assets available to General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it's more than just a kind of zero sum. There are assets; there are not assets. Availability is a key word. It seems relatively clear that this is an order related to close-air support and air support that augments the General's organic capability, right? So we speak in terms of organic and supporting assets. It also seems relatively clear that this capability is understood by the General to be ideally suited to support the close fight and to be responsive to his stated concern over the ability of the enemy to move, to manoeuvre, in depth to influence that close fight. So, yeah, I mean, there's no question that this indicates that he knew that he had close air support available, if he needed it. But I think one of the most significant pieces of information from the documents you have shown me is the percentage of strikes, 14.5 per cent pre-planned; 85.5, on order. When you see that, it suggests that the bulk of the capability was used to support the close fight, because it is being called in for close-air support purposes. It is not being used against pre-planned targets and that's logical, because air assets are inherently more responsive to manoeuvring enemy forces than indirect fire because they are responding to what the ground tactical commander is seeing as a threat or a developing situation. So I think, again, if you look at the entire body of information, I certainly agree with you that I didn't -- I wasn't aware of this when I made that comment about limited air assets.
