utterances.text: Then I would have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I was following the French translation. Could we all try to keep the speed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- down. Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies to the booth. If we're moving off that, I do believe that counsel has a 90(H) obligation to put his point concerning the use of these assets to the witness and whether or not that changes his assessment. That's an obligation counsel has. So before he moves off, I think it is incumbent upon the Prosecution to put their case on that score to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, Rule 90(H) has to do with witnesses who can give evidence. This witness doesn't have any evidence. All he has are opinions based on evidence which is fed to him. I don't have a 90(H) obligation to educate a witness and then ask him for an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then counsel shouldn't have conducted this cross. That flies in the face of what we have just been doing for the past two hours. The point of the matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to understand what has happened over the last -- well, let's say, the last half an hour. That is, that, apparently, Mr. Russo has put to the witness documentary evidence which the witness apparently had not considered when forming his opinions, and I did not get the impression that the witness contradicted the Prosecution's case. So apart from whether this is evidence in support of the Prosecution's case, or whether it is evidence which seeks to demonstrate the limited documentation available to this expert witness, apart from which of the two would be the right one, the obligation to put to the witness what the Prosecution's case is, is -- exists if the testimony given by the witness contradicts the Prosecution's case, if my understanding of Rule 90(H)(ii) is correct. Where, Mr. Kehoe, has this witness contradicted, during this testimony, the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First off, Mr. President, if we look at 90(H)(ii), it is not limited to fact witnesses in any fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that that was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was raised by counsel. He raised it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- that it was only limited to fact witnesses and the rule doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd -- first of all, if I could just respond to that. I didn't say that specifically. What I did say is that the rule relates, as can you see from the language, witnesses who are able to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And my position on that is evidence is, in fact, factual evidence, not legal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's -- let's leave that alone for the time being. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Secondly, the issue that counsel, after this examination, is going to argue, as sure as I'm standing here, is that the use of artillery by General Gotovina was unreasonable. That is the position that the Prosecution has taken in this case. And that he should have explored these air asserts to accomplish any goal he sought to accomplish, operationally and tactically, in the theatre of operations. If they're not going to argue that, then we would -- I ask for a stipulation on that. If they are, in fact, going argue, based on this evidence, that that was the way that General Gotovina should have gone, then 90(H) obliges them to "put to the witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears." And in that instance, it is Mr. Russo on behalf of the Prosecution, and if he is going to argue at the end of this case that General Gotovina should have used aircraft assets, be they fixed or rotor, as opposed to artillery, then that question should be put to Professor Corn in this proceeding before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, is that your position, that air asserts should have been used instead of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're not, at this point, under any obligation to tell the witness what we're going argue in our final trial brief. It is further not our obligation to indicate that he should have used this aircraft, that rotary helicopter. Our position is that his use of artillery was unreasonable. That is the case we have to put to the witness, and I believe he is well aware after that position, in fact, from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's check that. Are you aware that it's the Prosecution's case that artillery was used in an unreasonable way during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I understand that's their position. I certainly cannot help but draw the inference that the questions related to the availability of air assets are intended to suggest that that bolsters the position and so -- and undermines the opinion that I rendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber rules that the Prosecution has met its obligations under Rule 90(H)(ii). Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did just want to make one additional thing clear with respect to this particular line of questioning. It was, in addition to other things, to attack the witness's assertion in his report that General Gotovina's assets were essentially limited. I was simply attacking the basis for those assertions and demonstrating the witness's actual knowledge with respect to those particular areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that argument is part and parcel of the other argument, that the -- the only reason there is any relevance to that is if it has a corollary aspect that the use of rotor or fixed aircraft assets was something that should have been employed. Because if they are not connected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may finish this line. I didn't invite Mr. Russo to explain what he had done because the Chamber, of course, could observe what he did, and interprets his line of questioning accordingly. And apart from that, I think I already briefly referred to such a thing. So you may finish your -- you may finish your sentence. At the same time, the Chamber was not seeking any further argument on the ruling it already gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I think that the substance of my argument is present. I don't need to belabour the point. My apologies, if I did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, not your next comment but your next question is expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, looking back to your addendum at section 1, last paragraph on page 25, you state: "It seems clear that based on the METT-T-C General Gotovina would have to consider, use of a ground assault to destroy or disrupt enemy C3I in Knin would not have been a viable option." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you base that particular conclusion that a ground assault was not a viable option. What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first basis is the almost universal doctrinal principle that dismounted combat in urban environments is to be avoided really at almost all costs. It is understood, I think, in most armed forces, that it is a -- really an option of last resort. Because the urban environment grants to your defending opponent an exponential advantage as a result of the built-up terrain and degrades your ability to manoeuvre, to leverage fire support and air assets, and to have a clear picture of the battlefield. And if you recall from yesterday, I emphasised that a commander executing an operation has the primary objective of seizing and maintaining the initiative and dictating the tempo of the battle. Engaging an enemy in an urban environment cedes to the enemy initiative and tempo so it is to be avoided. Historically, you see this played out in, you know, universally known examples of the brutality of urban combat, like Stalingrad, and you also see it played out in interesting historical anecdotes, for example, the debate between General de Gaulle and Eisenhower over whether Paris should have been liberated or bypassed, with Eisenhower adamant that he did not want to engage in urban combat in Paris because of the detrimental impact he believed it would have operationally. And we know ultimately he lost that argument. This is a doctrinal axiom. So a prudent commander facing this requirement to destroy or, more importantly, to degrade military objectives within this urban terrain would instinctively be disinclined to engage in a ground assault. In addition, as I've said before, I think it is fairly clear that the General's priority of effort was the breach and destruction of the fixed enemy defensive positions. That is not an easy task. It's an extremely dangerous task. A commander would always prefer to attack an enemy in a meeting engagement as opposed to attacking an enemy in fixed positions. We see that the General -- I think you see that the General placed -- made that priority of effort manifest in his task to subordinate units. To conduct an urban assault, to set the conditions for the success of that priority of effort would have, in effect, shifted the priority of effort from the tactical point of attack to the supporting attack, because you couldn't have done it easily, or certainly that would have been a reasonable conclusion. The other factor is you have to look at the effect that he needed to achieve to set the conditions for the -- for the success of the priority of effort. The effect he needed to achieve was not to capture the headquarters. It was not to destroy the headquarters. It was to disrupt C3I, movement, mustering, resupply, and to create a sense of isolation for the enemy forces at the point of attack. That's my inference from everything I have seen related to the attack. And so if he had the mission, for example, if he felt that in order to succeed in this operation he had to actually capture the headquarters building, then that mission component of METT-T-C would have driven a different analysis. Because there are only certain assets that can capture people. Boots on the ground. But you have to assess how likely he would have considered the viability of a ground assault into Knin as a condition -- condition-setting supporting attack in light of the effect he needed to achieve to accomplish the mission. And when you put that together with the powerful kind of instinct or doctrinal underpinning that dismounted military operations in an urban environment are considered dangerous and to be avoided, then I think that would have been an unlikely course of action that he would have -- it would have been unlikely he would have considered that course of action viable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, I'm -- maybe we're thinking of different definitions of the term "viable." But before we get to that, was it your understanding that one of the objectives of Operation Storm was not to take the town of Knin?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was my understanding that the operation of objective Storm [sic] was to drive the enemy forces out of the area and capture their seat of command and control and government, which was Knin. That was the strategic objective. General Gotovina did what an operational commander is required to do. He translated the strategic objective into an operational course of action and he made the priority of effort for the operational execution defeat of the enemy defensive positions that were protecting that area, on the -- most likely on the assumption that once the enemy defences are defeated in depth, then the capturing of Knin will be facilitated substantially. So I'm not suggesting that he didn't realize at some point he might have to capture and control Knin. What I'm suggesting is that doesn't necessarily mean that he is going to set that as the first objective of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now in saying it is not a viable option, and it sounds maybe that you have a different definition or are employing a different definition. At least from my perspective, viable means, number one, first of all, whether can you do it. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible is one aspect of viable, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you -- when you say that it is not a viable option, I take it, based on your last answer, your second-last answer, is that even though it may have been possible, which you have not said, it certainly was not advisable. Is that fair or ...

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think advisable is a little bit misleading. First of all, I suspect it was possible. If the General had decided that the priority of effort of his corps was to capture the city, then I think you would have seen a radically different scheme of manoeuvre and a radically different emphasis for subordinate units. So when I say "not viable," what I mean is within the broader context of the priority of effort he set, it would have drawn -- it would have required a commitment of assets or certainly - make this clear - certainly he reasonably could have anticipated that it would have required a commitment of assets that would have functionally disabled all of the efforts he had made to make the priority of effort the tactical point of engagement with enemy defensive positions. And another aspect of this that relates to this use of the word "viable," one of the reasons dismounted operations in urban terrain is so disfavoured is because it is one of the most unpredictable combat battle spaces that a commander can confront. And predicting the flow of the battle is directly connected to tempo and maintaining initiative. So if General Gotovina had made a judgement that, I can take Knin with a battalion, and he commits that battalion, he is committing it with the full knowledge that he really can't predict whether that battalion will accomplish the mission. He can hope. But it's a different equation than a force-ratio analysis a commander would conduct in open terrain, or even against a fixed enemy defensive position. History demonstrates this. The problem for the commander is once he commits that force for that purpose, he's in a box. And another axiom of military operations is, never reinforce failure. All right? You have limited reinforcements, you reinforce success not failure. But that's a problem with urban terrain combat because you're almost sucked into the problem of having to reinforce failure because of the unpredictable nature of the operation, and this is why doctrinally it is so disfavoured and commanders are advised to seek alternate methods of addressing enemy positions in an urban environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Professor, before we move on to the details of a possible ground assault on Knin, you said, So if General Gotovina made a judgement that, Can I take Knin with a battalion, are you aware of what General Gotovina's assessment was at the time, concerning the viability of taking Knin with troops?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because my review of the information indicates that he made the judgement that he wasn't going to make that the priority of effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P461. And if we could go to page 10 in the English and page 19 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm looking at a portion where General Gotovina says -- first of all, Professor, this is the Brioni transcript, which I believe you're familiar with. General Gotovina's statement: "The forces heading towards Knin are 400 good infantrymen from the 3rd Battalion, the 126th Regiment, who are all from this area and they know the area through and through. They have reason to fight here and at this moment it is difficult to keep them on a leash. There is the 1st Croatian Zdrug, which has 300 infantrymen, which has proved itself in this area at this moment, and in any case, we can count on those infantrymen. There are special units of the Croatian and Herceg-Bosna MUP, which have 350 excellent infantrymen, who have shown themselves to be outstanding in the operation. That means that we have somewhere around 1.000 good infantrymen, trained for assault operations, for quick transfers on this difficult terrain; we can easily take Knin without any problem." Now, Professor, if General Gotovina made the assessment that he could easily and without any problem take Knin with these thousand men, what is your basis or do you have a basis for disagreeing with him?

utterances.speaker: GEOFFREY CORN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I have read this and I think this is really quite significant. Again, you put it in broader context and it creates maybe a different impression. In the paragraph antecedent to this paragraph, the president is talking about placing Knin under fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And placing Knin direct -- operations directly in -- towards Knin. Now, in the -- when I read this, it jumped out at me for the reason you suggest, because it seems to think that here's the General saying, I'm just ready to march into Knin and take it over. I think other aspects of this document support the conclusion that there are different voices in this meeting but the tenor of the General's voice is operational execution, close with and destroy the enemy. It is manifest in a couple of places. I assume this document's been admitted into evidence, is that -- okay. So the Trial Chamber will obviously have seen it and make that judgement. It says, Please remember how many Croatian villages and towns have been destroyed. But that's still not the situation in Knin today. There's a counter-attack in Knin and so forth. It would provide a very good justification for this action ... we have a pretext to strike ... Now here is the operational commander listening to the political leader basically saying, you know, as part of planning this tactical destruction of enemy armed forces, look for an opportunity to inflict damage on the city, and the commander responds, in my view, one reasonable way to interpret this is to kind of push that back, Mr. President, don't worry about Knin. I can take Knin when I have to, right? I have got forces. I'm capable of doing it. But the General, through this whole discussion, is talking about the tactical destruction of enemy forces. And obviously, if I'm the commanding general and I know that I have defeated the enemy in depth, then the dominos start falling and I will be able to walk into Knin, because once those frontline positions are breached and defeated, then the leadership in Knin knows that the outcome is inevitable, and I'm dictating the terms. So, again, I think there -- it is possible to read this as General Gotovina saying, As part of my plan, I'm ready to just march into Knin. But I think in the broader context, it suggests something quite different, which is he is trying to push the president off of this kind of overzealous pressure to put Knin under fire. And part of my reason for saying that is something we talked about previously, which is he had the capability to do this for some time, to just rain fire on Knin. Now, I mean, there're, again, multiple reasons why he might not have exploited that opportunity. If you -- I think if you look at this, he comes out of this meeting, orders are prepared, annexes are prepared, tasks for subordinate units, priorities of effort, and it all points to the same operational judgement, I'm going use my ground tactical capability, my close air support, my MiG -- my Mi-24s, which are anti-armour, anti-personnel aircraft. I'm going to leverage all that to the best I can at the priority of effort, which is defeating the enemy ground tactical capability in depth. In order to do that, I have to set conditions related to their support structure and I will use assets that I think can do it. So that was my reaction to that when I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I'm looking at the clock. We have to conclude for the day. Professor Corn, you are not available tomorrow, from what we understand. We'd like to see you back on Thursday, the 10th of September, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II. And my instruction to you is the same as yesterday, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. For the parties, we'll hear testimony through videolink tomorrow. We adjourn and we will resume Wednesday, the 9th of September, 9.00, Courtroom I.
